1.	Has the government of Canada recently borrowed 35 million dollars from the banks at 4 per cent for a term of two years?
2.	To what extent did the banks borrow under the Finance Act from the government in the year ending September 30, 1932?
3. What rate of interest was charged the banks by the government for the amount borrowed, referred to in question No. 2?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will read the answer to that question.
Some of the reactions to the report that the government had arranged a sale to the banks of $35,000,000 in two-year notes which the banks would use as security for borrowing under the Finance Act appear to indicate some misunderstanding of the situation. So far as I am aware the best and most conservative opinion throughout the world is committed to the idea that an easing of money and credit is highly desirable in the interests of business recovery. Such is certainly the case in Great Britain and in the United States.
The credit situation in Great Britain has been materially improved. In the United States a recent enactment gives power to the National banks to create new note issues aggregating nearly $1,000,000,000 against the security of certain classes of government bonds, and this measure supplemented a central bank policy of easing money, which resulted in bringing the government bond holdings of the Federal Reserve system to a figure in excess of $1,800,000,000.
While it may be said that the positive benefits of such actions have still to be achieved there is no question that they have prevented the situation from becoming decidedly worse. In such matters no one can afford to disregard the judgment of the two leading financial countries of the world, although in our case it has to be interpreted in the light of our own situation which differs materially from that of Great Britain on the one hand and of the United States on the other.
In the case of Canada the only machinery available for action along these lines is found in the Finance Act. In the recent transaction the banks purchased two year notes -of the Dominion of Canada, bearing interest at the rate of 4 per cent, and these notes the banks will use as security in obtaining an advance of an equivalent amount under the Finance Act, thereby swelling their cash reserves and substantially increasing their loaning capacity. This procedure differs in technique, but not in fact, from normal central bank policies followed in various other countries.
Because of our sound banking situation a Canadian policy of this type can and must be of a much more restricted character both relatively and absolutely than the examples to which I have referred. In fact, advances under the Finance Act are today at a very low level. At the close of business on November 7 such advances amounted to only $28,344,000 and when full advantage is taken of the recent arrangement the total will only slightly exceed $40,000,000.
Reference to the monthly return of the chartered banks will show that each autumn in recent years operations under the Finance Act have assumed important proportions. Thus, at the end of November, 1931, they totalled $66,500,000, while on the same date in 1930 the figure was $38,700,000 and in 1929 SI 12,900.000. Not only are advances under the Finance Act at a low level but our gold holdings are larger than a year ago. Today our gold holdings represent 44-5 per cent of the-total dominion note circulation as compared with 43-1 per cent on the same date last year.
Out of the proceeds of the $35,000,000 loan, $12,000,000 was used immediately to retire a short term debt. The balance was used to supplement the Receiver General banking accounts which each year on November 1 must be adequate not -only to provide for the ordinary operations of the various branches of the public service, but also to pay approximately $30,000,000 of interest on our national debt.. Once the present 4 per cent loan operation is completed, the dominion is finished with the market for some time to come. There are no more temporary loans to redeem, and the next maturity is in August, 1933.
After having proved our ability to ride out the storm, I feel that we were justified-to the-

Second Narrows Bridge
ter a question concerning a matter which has been before the government 'for some time. What action, if any, has the government decided to take in restoring the span of the Second Narrows bridge?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be within the memory of hon. members that the Second Narrows bridge, so-called, in the harbour of Vancouver was practically destroyed by the centre span falling into the river in consequence of an accident. The decision of the court of last resort involved certain liability against the bridge company. The bridge company however received from this parliament last year an extension of its charter and subsequently went into liquidation, a receiver being appointed, the operations of the company from that time forward being directed by the courts.
A contract was let for the construction of a new superstructure, also for the construction of a lift span, that being the type of span recommended by Sir Alexander Gibb as the one best fitted to meet the difficulties of navigation at that point. Difficulties however were experienced in connection with financing and finally, with the acquiescence of the government, the bridge is being turned over to the harbour commissioners for the purpose of enabling them to do what may be necessary to render suitable accommodation, and to allow them to erect a suitable structure so that navigation may not be interfered with. That will be done under the direction of the court. Tnder the liquidation, the court being asked to approve, of course, every possible step is being taken to bring about the construction of the bridge. Negotiations are not completed, but they are proceeding along those lines.
I may say to hon. members that the bridge in question is a toll bridge, located in the very centre of Vancouver harbour. The harbour commissioners of that city will be charged with the responsibility of operating and maintaining the bridge, under a deed of trust which will ensure its return to those who originally owned it, namely the municipalities at either side of the narrows, when the obligations have been discharged to -the harbour commissioners and to the municipalities that advanced $630,000. That is a general outline of what is being done. Details have not been settled, however, and negotiations are being completed. The law officers of the
crown are supervising, on behalf of the harbour commissioners, what has been agreed upon, to see that it is put into proper legal form, and that the courts of the province under whose direction the receiver acts give proper directions in the premises.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with the statement made by the Prime Minister concerning the reconstruction of (he Second Narrows bridge, which is being done under the direction of the harbour commissioners of Vancouver, may I ask whether advances will be made by the government to the harbour commissioners for that purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The city of Vancouver sent a telegram to the government indicating that they would take $300,000 worth of the security. The harbour commissioners of Vancouver have a very substantial reserve, and so far as we are advised at the present time they will be able to finance the undertaking.
Has not the government changed or altered its policy as expressed one or two years ago, namely, that it would not contribute anything to the erection of toll bridges ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No; the conveyance of the undertaking is being made to the harbour commissioners; they will be the proprietors of the property in trust, until such time as the obligations of the bridge company have been discharged.

Hon. R. J. MANiION (Minister of Railways and Canals): The question the hon. member has brought up is a very complicated one. I presume most members of this house, those who come from railway centres at any rate, have received many such letters as the one the hon. gentleman has read-

subtopic: DISTRIBUTION OF WORK IN THE OPERATING TRADES
speechtext: Hundreds of them.

subtopic: DISTRIBUTION OF WORK IN THE OPERATING TRADES
speechtext:
-and also others from the other side, that is, from the senior railway-men. The fact is that the government has no power whatever in this matter unless the government, or some government, chose to overrule the agreements between the men's unions and the railway companies, for it affects both railway companies alike. I may say that I have asked the railway companies for their side of the question, and quite frankly both railways, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, take the position that they have agreements with the men's unions and that they do not care to interfere with those 53719-59J
agreements. The senior men who are getting what the other men claim to be excess mileage take the position that these agreements stand, and they object to any interference with them. It is a matter wholly between the two railway companies and the unions as representing the men.
Of course, men who are out of employment, the junior men, those who as the railwaymen express it are "bumped off,"-I think that is quite the proper railway expression,-by the senior men, naturally protest. The senior men on the other hand take the attitude that they have rights, to make up to, say, 4,800 miles on a passenger train and 4,000 on a freight train. And they have a further argument which complicates the matter, namely that their pension is based upon the earnings of the last ten years of their service, and if they should give up some of their time it cuts down their pension. Incidentally many of the men's unions take the attitude, and I think truthfully, that they have already given up a certain mileage to the men who are not employed, and thereby have spread the work.
' Without being too verbose I have tried to show some of the difficulties of the situation. I repeat that the government has no power to interfere, it is a matter between the railway companies and the men themselves, and while the government has passed on these representations to the railway companies, the companies have so far taken the attitude that they will not or cannot move in the matter.

The British preferential tariff cannot apply, nor can any of the provisions thereunder apply to such goods, so that we shall be obliged to fall back on section 2 of article I, which provides that the goods must come directly into Canada. speechtext: My hon. friend will pardon me if I am unusually blunt in my answer. He will persist in building up imaginary cases. I tried to answer him yesterday as clearly as I could in the English language, and I will try to do so again. As regards goods coming in from South Africa under the British preferential rate, they enjoy all the privileges that accrue to shipments under that rate. Secondly, the term direct shipment to which he has referred in the regulation by the department is a well-recognized, well-established and standardized meaning in this country, accepted and understood by every customs administrator and officer, and it includes, so far as South Africa is concerned, the movement of goods to Canada which may be transshipped from one ship to another at Great Britain en route, provided it is perfectly clear by the documentation of the goods that they are destined for Canada. My hon, friend raises this bogy. He says if these articles- apricots, pineapples, cape gooseberries, plums, figs, quinces and so on-came under the British preferential tariff, they would enjoy certain privileges. But he says they are not coming in under that, so that they will lose those privileges. Let us see what the facts are in regard to these items which the hon. gentleman cites by way of illustration to support his views. Under the British preference these goods would pay 2 cents per pound; under the treaty they pay 1 cent per pound. So that so far as they are concerned they get the advantage under the treaty. As regards direct shipment, they will be treated precisely the same as goods coming under the British preference. I hope I have made that clear.

speechtext:
I ask that
question because I notice that there is a difference in the two clauses of the agreement which relate to the benefits to be given by respective countries under this treaty.

South Africa
As regards South Africa, if they are to get the benefit of the preference on goods shipped into this country, they must come direct. I understand the minister to say, now, that "direct" can be given a broad interpretation, which will serve the same purpose. But when one reads the clause relating to goods going from Canada to South Africa, to enjoy the benefit of the preference in South Africa, the clause distinctly states, they may come direct, or that they may be transshipped, and it does not confine transshipment to transshipment in Great Britain. They may be transshipped at any point. All that is necessary is to satisfy the customs officer that the original intention was to ship the goods from Canada to South Africa. Can my hon. friend explain why there is that difference between the two clauses-why they were not worded in the same way?

The answer is quite simple. In each case, and in all these treaties, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and so forth, we have always endeavoured to carry into the provision the nomenclature of the laws governing the countiy where the goods enter. That is to say, where we have an established practice in 'Canada we endeavour to word the article in the treaty governing the movement of goods into Canada in accordance with the general practice in this country; and the reverse is the case with respect to the other dominions. In both instances, these articles conform to and harmonize with the established practice in the respective dominions. And may I explain why that is so. It will be readily understood that if we inject into the treaty terminology which will call for a course of action different from the common practice, it involves a certain amount of confusion in administrative circles. In other words, as I said to my hon. friend a moment ago, the tendency is to standardize the laws or regulations which govern the movement of goods. We have been complying with the standardized practice in Canada and at the other end with the standardized practice in South Africa.

I am afraid that the nomenclature and terminology, so far as Canada is concerned, appears to be of a restrictive character. That is the point to which I wish to call attention. It is another form of restricting rather than of enlarging trade facilities. According to what my hon. friend has just said, the Canadian government apparently requires shipments direct. The other parts of the empire, particularly South Africa, as in this case, do not require direct shipment, but permit transshipment and expressly so deolare. In other words, they are seeking to encourage trade, whereas, by our nomenclature or terminology, we have another device for restricting trade.
Is the minister not simply saying that when an importer brings in goods on a through bill of lading, it makes no difference what route they follow?
That is not precisely correct.
In the case of goods shipped on a through bill of lading from South Africa to Montreal what difference would it make whether they came via Great Britain or via New York?

There is a very marked distinction. If the goods are shipped from South Africa on a through bill of lading but are transshipped at London to a British, Canadian or any other ship direct to a Canadian port, they are admissible; if they are shipped on a through bill of lading and transshipped at London for New York, they do not then earn the privileges accruing under the treaty.
Why should that ibe so?
Those who had the matter in hand desired to maintain as far as possible the movement of trade through the expensive ports which have been developed in this country.

I would call the minister'3 attention to item 549, which reads:
Wool, the hair of the camel, alpaca, goat, or other like animal not further prepared than combed:
Provided that importations under this item, wholly the product of any British country, when imported direct from the United Kingdom into a sea, lake or river port of Canada, shall be entitled to the benefits of the British preferential tariff.

Both these items are composite items made up of a number of different articles classified under the term wool in one case, and hides, in the other. As I stated last night the reason this is carried into the treaty is to make it clear that these items are subject to precisely the terms contained in the general tariff act. As I said a moment ago to the

Which clause is that?

Section 2 of article I. This section says distinctly that the benefits shall accrue on goods imported directly into Canada. Goods are no more imported directly into Canada when they come from Capetown to Liverpool and then to Montreal than if they come from Capetown to Montreal or from Capetown to Portland and then by rail to Montreal. I have no argument with my hon. friend as to his method but I do contend that this article does not contain the interpretation put upon it by the minister. I think the importer should know what he can and cannot do.
Has the minister the regulation which does apply that interpretation?

Last evening we had a
very lengthy discussion upon this matter and I pointed out to hon. gentlemen who were asking precisely the same question now raised that the term "direct shipment" had through practice and regulation been given a certain definite meaning. I have under my hand a copy of an order in council dated December 1, 1926. I shall read only part thereof, but will hand it to Hansard so that it may appear in full. It reads:
At The Government House At Ottawa Wednesday, the 1st day of December, 1926.
Present:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council
Whereas by section 1 of chapter 7 of the statutes of 1926, paragraph 1 of section 3 of The Customs Tariff, 1907, was repealed and a new paragraph substituted:
And whereas the Minister of Finance reports that the effect of the substitution was that in 
order to enjoy the benefits of the British preferential tariff, goods must be conveyed without transshipment from the port of any British country enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff into a sea or river port of Canada, whereas formerly goods might enjoy the said privileges when imported direct from any British country;
Now therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in . Council, in order to secure a uniform administration of tariff laws, is pleased, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, to order and it is hereby ordered that the words "direct shipment" or words meaning direct shipment, wherever they occur in The Customs Tariff or in any trade agreement, shall as respects goods imported into Canada on and after the first day of April, 1927, from any British country entitled to admission into Canada at rates as low as or lower than the British preferential tariff, be held to mean conveyed into a sea or river port of Canada on a bill of lading from the country of origin, showing the ultimate destination to be Canada, without contingency of diversion, and without transshipment except at a port of any British country enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff.
His Excellency in Council is further pleased to order that order in council of the 15th November, 1926 (P.C. 1832) be and it is hereby cancelled.
(Sgd.) E. J. Lemaire, Clerk of the Privy Council.

Could the minister tell us whether South Africa has any anti-dumping legislation which would prevent the Canadian manufacturer selling cream separators cheaper in South Africa than in Canada?

South Africa, in common with practically all countries, has a provision that when any import obviously of a dumping character, interferes with its internal interests, action may be taken to prevent its intrusion in the market.
May I ask the minister a question which I think has been asked before: Is there any provision with respect to the labour content or material content of goods manufactured in Canada?

I answered that question last night. There is no specific provision in any of these agreements. The practice or rule governing the various countries operates, as it does at the present, subject to whatever change may be desired. In regard to most of the countries comprised within the British Empire, an empire content of fifty per cent may be accepted as a general rule. But there are, of course, variations. In the case of the mother country it is twenty-five per cent. In the case of the Dominion of Canada, it is generally speaking fifty per cent with the exception of certain articles, such as cottons, where it is thirty-three and a third. Certain variations have been found necessary, according to the nature of the article. In some cases such as cotton, where all the raw material is imported and where its value constitutes a substantial portion of the ultimate cost, then necessarily the empire content must be lowered. In other instances, where the raw material is partly or wholly produced within the empire or within the country, the empire [DOT]content can be raised just as easily. That [DOT]was one of the problems which faced the conference in its attempt to adopt a uniform measure. The matter is still under consideration and study by the various dominions as *well as the mother country.
What about motor cars?

Motor cars are pretty well standardized in various parts of the empire. It will be recalled that Australia and New Zealand maintain a dual content with certain tariff rates applicable thereto. Fifty per cent carries a lower rate than 75 per cent, and the same thing applies in other parts of the empire.

South Africa
Would the minister tell me what change, if any, is made in the tariff by the present arrangement with regard to item 134 in schedule B?

I dealt with that very fully last night. The British preference varies according to degrees, and I hope my hon. friend will not ask me to go into all the different degrees, of which there are about twenty.
No, I do not want all the details, if the minister can just give me the general effect.

South Africa gets the
British preferential rate. We had a very long discussion on this matter last night.
I am referring to schedule B; I think the minister is referring to schedule A.
My hon. friend is talking about the South African item?
Yes.

On item 134(a) the minimum is free and the maximum one shilling per hundred pounds. We get the minimum. On item 134(b) the minimum is free and the maximum 8 pence per hundred pounds. We get the minimum. On item 134(d) the minimum is 15 per cent and the maximum 20 per cent. We get the minimum. On item 134(e) the minimum is free and the maximum 5 per cent. We get the minimum. On item 134(g) the minimum is 15 per cent and the maximum 20 per cent. We get the minimum. On item 134(h) the minimum is free and the maximum 3 shillings each. We get the minimum.
I wonder if the minister has the same information with regard to item 270(b). If it has been given already and is on Hansard I can get it there.

No, I do not think it has been dealt with. There is no change in that item at present; the question is still under consideration by the government of South Africa. The rate there is 5 per cent minimum and 5 per cent maximum. We are guaranteed the lowest rate, but the matter was not settled by the delegation when they were here, as to what spread would be given.
Is it still a matter of negotiation?

The matter is open for them to act, and in this and a number of other items something may be done. They are under no obligation to make any changes, but if such changes are made we are guaranteed the minimum.
With regard to those items in schedule B on which we get the lowest rate given any country, have we any control over what that lowest rate may be? It might be a very high rate.

We are in precisely the
same position as are all other countries; we control our own rates but we do not control the rates in other countries. There is no question about that, and there is no use beating about the bush. We have no control over their rates, but we are guaranteed the lowest rate that any country receives.

I understand that the government has no control over the rates in other countries, but I am reminded of the argument of the Prime Minister two years ago, with regard to countervailing duties against the United States. The right hon. gentleman said then that our tariff policy would be dictated by other countries. In connection with these items on which we get the lowest rate given any country it would seem that we are to be dictated to by those countries, and we do not know what the rates will be.

Is this not the same
principle that was contained in the treaty with France with regard to wheat? We were to receive the lowest duty given any country in the world, but there was a great deal of complaint in the house because we did not say definitely what would be the duty, and France increased it.

I could not hear what the
hon. member for Willow Bunch said, but I think he was asking whether this is not the same principle to which objection was taken in connection with the French treaty. There is no limit to the height to which the government of South Africa might raise their tariff against us; there is no provision here which will prevent them from raising it. I should like to ask the minister if that is not correct, and if it is not correct also that we have bound ourselves not to raise our tariff against South Africa.

I thought we had fully
covered that point. It will be observed that in connection with a certain number of items enumerated in schedule B we are to be given the lowest rate. The point really is this: The government of South Africa, in the spirit which actuated the negotiations here, are desirous of giving to the British Empire the minimum tariff rate. In some cases there might be a competition between Canada and Australia in the South African market-in-

deed, that competition does exist-and in other cases there might be competition there between Canada and Great Britain. In these cases the term "lowest rate to any country" is used. At least it ensures that position to us. We are satisfied to compete in the South African market on that basis in connection with these articles to which that term applies. We feel ourselves competent to compete with these other countries, and we are satisfied with that position. I see no reason for alarm at all.

Does that mean any
country in the world or any one of the dominions?

It means precisely what

Then I take it that South

We have done a good

Can the minister cite an instance where that has been done?

I have not the precise data under my hand. I could bring files that would keep us busy for a week, but I may make this statement, speaking from memory. In the *central American republics, Colombia and [DOT]Panama, and in Cuba, where there has been a *considerable market, we have made some progress as also in some of the other sections of the West Indies. We are discussing the South African treaty at the moment, and I do not think that the question of potatoes has been very definitely considered in this regard. However, I will make a note of the question and look into it.

What progress has been made in negotiations with England with regard [DOT]to the embargo on potatoes?

Yes.

With respect to all the

expect to export peas, com and tomatoes in tins or otherwise to South Africa when we have to meet the competition of the world, if ;ur manufacturers need a high tariff on these /ery products when they are marketing them right here in Canada? Twenty per cent.

Would not that be an indication that perhaps the tariff on these items-
I mean the Canadian tariff-might be reduced?

I wish to state two or

There are certain points which strike me quite forcibly and about which I should like to comment, but I do not intend to take up too much time in a discussion thereof.
The first has been mentioned already by the minister. We are expected to be able to compete satisfactorily in South Africa on even terms with other countries, but in this country these same manufacturers are protected to a large extent. That is a rather significant situation.
So far as I can see and unless some statement has been made in which good faith is involved, there is nothing to prevent South Africa extending these lowest rates not only to other members of the British Empire, in which case it would be a preferential rate, but to any other country in the world. Any preference we receive with regard to these items is dependent upon the policies adopted by South Africa towards other countries. This does not debar South Africa from lowering her rates to other countries to any degree she wishes at any time during the next five years. This question, which I think is very important, then arises: To how many countries are these special rates extended, with what countries must we compete under these rates at the present time and with what countries must we compete in the future? It seems to me that in the case of seventeen out of fifty-two items we have received no preference; all we have received is a guarantee that we shall be permitted to meet any country in the world on equal terms in open competition.

My hon. friend does not
state the case quite fairly; I think he just reverses the application of this agreement.

Was there any discussion
as to the possibility of finding a market in South Africa for our dairy products?

I think it would be unprofitable for us to go into a lengthy exploration of that problem. Offhanded, I would say that there is not very much chance, except in the case of our excellent Canadian cheese. I doubt if butter could be exported to South Africa considering the long haul through the tropics.
Australia and New Zealand export to South Africa.

Australia and especially
New Zealand have developed a highly intensified dairying industry. Canada's major external market is Great Britain, the largest butter market in the world. How about condensed
milk?

There are possibilities in
the case of condensed milk and other manufactured products of that kind.

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 8, respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the progress of the debate upon the resolution upon which this bill was founded, I think the whole matter was so fully discussed as to make it unnecessary for me to do more than refer to one or two points about which there seems to have been some difficulty on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite. It will be observed that at page 911 of Hansard the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) is reported as follows:-
When we look at the United Kingdom agreement as defined in Great Britain and find that we receive only free entry, but no agreement that the duties are to be kept up or imposed against the rest of the world, and compare with that our agreement W'hich provides that the margin of preference shall be maintained, and that the present tariff rates on one hundred and fifty-nine articles are to be pegged for five years, wre immediately realize the difference.
I think it has been made abundantly clear that in the agreement entered into between the United Kingdom and the Dominion of Canada there are certain items, largely agricultural, with respect to which we have a clear, definite and guaranteed preference for a period of five years. The first concession established by this agreement is that there shall be free entry for all products except a small number specified in the existing tariffs of Great Britain when the Import Duties Act was passed in March, 1932. We are to have free entry into the markets of the United Kingdom. Article I establishes that so clearly that were it not for the observations which have been made and which I cannot understand, I would not now read it. It reads as follows:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom undertake that orders shall be made in accordance with the provisions of section 4 of the Import Duties Act, 1932, which will ensure the continuance after the 15th November, 1932, of entry free of duty into the United Kingdom of goods consigned from any part of the British Empire and grown, produced or manufactured in Canada which by virtue of that act are now free of duty subject, however, to the reservations set forth in schedule A appended hereto.

United Kingdom
It follows that with the exception of the items mentioned in Schedule A free entry is established for all the products of this dominion into the markets of Great Britain.

With respect to Schedule A which limits to three years the provisions which I have just read and which would otherwise be extended for five years, it is only necessary to look at the language of that schedule in order to remove all possible doubts. It reads:
As regards eggs, poultry, buttter, cheese and other milk products, free entry for Canadian produce will be continued for three years certain. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, however, reserve to themselves the right, after the expiration of the three years, if they consider it necessary in the interests of the United Kingdom producer to do so, to review' the basis of preference so far as relates to the articles above enumerated and, after notifying His Majesty's government in Canada either to impose a preferential duty on Canadian produce -whilst maintaining preferential margins, or in consultation with the Canadian government to bring such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom markets.
Not the preference, but the basis of the preference:
-so far as relates to the articles above enumerated and, after notifying His Majesty's government in Canada either to impose a preferential duty on Canadian produce whilst maintaining preferential margins, or in consultation with the Canadian government to bring such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom market.
I can hardly find it possible -to think that there should have been differences of opinion as to what is meant by that schedule. We have in article 1 provision for free entry for a period of five years, but with respect to eggs and poultry, butter, cheese and other milk products that free entry is for three years certain, but the preference is to be extended for the remaining two years of that agreement. That preference in terms of that schedule may be expressed (a) by a duty against Canadian products as well as against foreign products, but with the maintenance of a preference in favour of Canadian products; that is, to re-53719-80
view, not the preference, but the basis of the preference only; and (b), and this is so clear that there need be no doubt, a quota system, and whatever quota system there may be, it must be arrived at in consultation with the government of Canada.
Then comes the provision with respect -to legislation to be passed to secure for Canada a certain position with respect to items therein specified:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to impose on the foreign goods specified in schedule B appended hereto, the duties of customs shown in that schedule in place of the duties (if any) now leviable.
In other words, there is a specified list of goods which for five years will find entry into the British market on a preference basis indicated in the terms of schedule B. That is, whatever may be the price of wheat, for instance, it will have to pay two shillings a quarter to find a market in Great Britain if it comes from a foreign country whereas coming from a British dominion it enters free. It is important in view of what was said last evening that I read again on to the record, in order that there be no doubt, just what items are covered by the five-year guarantee with particular reference to the agricultural products. I need hardly say that in the framing of these agreements it was found neither necessary nor desirable that there should be duplication, or that- there should be repeated in the Australian agreement, for instance, all the items that received this guaranteed preferential treatment in the Canadian agreement, and conversely, it was not necessary to place in the Canadian agreement all these items that received preferential treatment from Australia, and the same applies to South Africa and New Zealand; for the benefits accorded in respect of any one item in the form of a guaranteed preference for five years to any one of the dominions accrue, of course, to the benefit of all the others. Let us have no misapprehension as to the extent of that list and the character of the preference granted. These have been worked out with great care with respect to all the countries that may be concerned.

Our potatoes have that benefit subject, of course, to this:	At the bottom of all these
agreements there must be freedom from disease of the potatoes or cattle or of anything else. In the granting of preferences, no question should ever arise of granting a preference to invade a market within the British dominions with diseased products, whatever they may be. With respect to potatoes, Great Britain has spent very large sums of money in making it impossible for the Colorado beetle to find lodgment in that country. At one spot in France the Colorado beetle was imported in a bag of potatoes, with the result that France had to spend very large sums of money in stamping out the evil that arose by reason of the Colorado beetle finding lodgment in their country. Great Britain has been extremely anxious about the health of potatoes, or perhaps I had better say, about the sound condition of the potatoes imported, because they have been fearful that the Colorado beetle would find lodgment in their country. Finally we arranged with them, believing as we do that the precautions we take are ample to prevent the possibility of the Colorado beetle finding lodgment in Great Britain, and I believe my

hon. friend from Prince would think it was desirable that we should do so, to send one of their experts over here to observe the method in which potatoes are packed in this country for shipment. In other words, we think we can demonstrate beyond peradven-ture that there is little or no opportunity for the potato bug to find a place in shipments of potatoes from this country to the detriment of the country that is importing our potatoes. Be that as it may, I think their expert is already in this country observing the method by which we prepare our potatoes for shipment. I for one, if I were living in England, would not for a moment doubt the desirability of preventing by every means in my power the lodgment of the Colorado beetle in that country, and the efforts they have made and the money they have expended, and will continue to make and expend, for the purpose of freeing their country from that dreaded scourge so far as potatoes are concerned, is a sufficient indication that it is something more than a misapprehension that they have. Then, the schedule refers to fresh fish, salmon, other fish canned, asbestos and so on. The articles in schedule C are to receive the preference as indicated. Now, that preference is an 53719-60 J

So we have first, the free entry for everything, with the exception of a small number of items that carry tariff rates, to which I referred in my opening statement, and a few other items, unimportant so far as we are concerned at the moment, against which duties were imposed some years ago. That is, free entry is the general rule. Then in schedule B, with respect to that vast number of items which constitute our agricultural products, we have a preference in the United Kingdom market guaranteed for five years. We have in schedule C a further preference guaranteed for five years with respect to a certain number of agricultural and other raw products. By schedule A it is provided in respect of a few articles that free entry is to be maintained for three years certain, the preference thereafter to be continued for another two years either by a margin of tariff by way of preference, or by a quota.

These are the general points, without going into detail, because I put upon Hansard when presenting the resolution upon which this bill is based a detailed statement of the situation. We recognize that in connection with food products and certain mineral products, where the products of the dominion are more than ample to meet the requirements of Great Britain, where there is an export surplus beyond what will meet the requirements of the United Kingdom, the world's prices prevail. And those world prices are the prices which must determine the price charged on first sale. I shall not labour the question which has been so well covered, but would state that first sale means, and has always meant, the first purchase or the first sale of the commodity of a purchaser. That is the first sale. That first sale price must be the world's supply and demand price, and about that I suppose there can be no doubt in the mind of any hon. member in the house. In the absence of a premium on account of quality, the world's supply and demand price would prevail.
In this instance we have said that with respect to the Dominion of Canada we are

content that our agricultural people and our mineral producers should meet any markets or any producers in the world in the markets of Great Britain. Having done that we are accorded a preference on copper, zinc, lead, asbestos and wheat. So that the foreigner, whoever he may be, or from whatever country he may come, who desires to place his product in the market of Great Britain, through any port, will have to pay, before he does so, the amount I have indicated- whether he be selling wheat, flour, mineral products, or any other products I have mentioned. That is the position.
Those are the terms which have been made, and I believe such terms should commend themselves to the judgment of Canadians. There may be differences of opinion, but at any rate those are the facts. Then the United Kingdom agreed that with respect to our cattle she would pass the necessary legislation to permit the landing of our cattle on terms competitive with those of the Irish Free State. It will fee understood that that legislation has already been passed, and the bargain in that regard has been implemented. Then, further, the government of the United Kingdom agreed that it would deal with the pork industry on a basis which would be satisfactory to Canadians. I have heard many adverse criticisms with respect to the provisions regarding pork and the pig industry. Perhaps hon. members opposite will recall, and I have no doubt many hon. members do, that from a political standpoint the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier regarded pork as more important than wheat.
What was the position? We have Great Britain called upon to decide whether or not they would deal with their domestic producers either by a tariff preference or by a quota preference. For a long time the agitation in favour of a .tariff preference seemed to be in the ascendant, but later it became clear that the British government had concluded that a quota preference with respect to the pork industry was more desirable than a tariff preference. With that in mind they appointed a commission, and the report of that commission has been made since the opening of this session. Under that report the quota system has been-or at least will be established, because the recommendation of the commission is to that effect. This dominion is to find itself on an equality with the British producer, and under the quota system we will be allotted up to 2,500,000 hundredweight per annum. I need hardly point out to you, sir, that this is a larger quantity than this country has ever exported into Great Britain, and it affords an ample margin for any develop-

ment that may take place in the industry in Canada; so large a margin in fact that we would have to increase our production many times over what it has been in order that it might be met. I regard that as of first rate importance. Notwithstanding what has been said by hon. gentlemen apposite, we find that this Dominion of Canada has secured in the market of the greatest importing community to which we can possibly have access a freedom for the distribution of its pork products in terms similar to those of the British producer, to the extent of two and a half million hundredweight per annum. That wre regard as a very important provision of the agreement.
Then we come to another article of commerce, namely tobacco. In 1923 the matter was under discussion in Great Britain. Later the British government enacted legislation that provided for a tariff-or a preference, we will put it that way-of two shillings and a halfpenny per pound, or approximately fifty cents. Now the price of tobacco in this country has fluctuated from eighteen to forty cents. The price this year runs from eighteen to twenty-four cents, I think. In the neighbouring republic the price runs from twelve and a half to fifteen cents a pound. We Canadians are now to have in the market of Great Britain, a market of 40,000,000 people, a preference of substantially fifty cents a pound for the next ten years on tobacco. I may point out to this house that experiments in western Ontario have indicated that the quality of flue-cured tobacco there produced has been extraordinarily fine, and that the production has gone as high as one thousand pounds per acre. The average in Rhodesia, in India and in the United States has not been in excess of five hundred pounds per acre. So that the Canadian, with his higher rate of production, and a tariff preference of fifty cents a pound, is afforded an opportunity of which I think he has not been slow to avail himself. That is during the years that are past, when the same rate of duty prevailed-and I do not say for a moment that the duty has been changed, for it has not; it is the same fifty cent rate that was established in, I think, 1923 or 1925-

speechtext:
That was renewed, and now we have it extended for the further period of ten years. We oannot but think that will be of the greatest possible benefit to the Canadian producer.
That in a general way constitutes what we receive, in addition to the provision that has been made in connection with the self-governing colonies and protectorates, who are to

United Kingdom
accord to this dominion any preference which may for the time being be granted to any other part of the British Empire, with limitations in connection with the political conditions in South Africa. Against that what have we agreed to do?
But before I pass to that, my friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) reminds me that I should point out the provision that has been made with respect to fair competition. It will be recalled that our timber was subject to unfair competition from Russia. It will also be recalled that other Canadian products were subject to like unfair competition. I once gave this house an illustration with respect to asbestos, I think. There is a small asbestos mine in the eastern townships of the province of Quebec. The output of asbestos from that mine was taken entirely by one customer in the United States. The gentleman who is the president of the enterprise told me this himself in this city, when he happened to be here in connection with other matters. For years they had taken the entire product of that, asbestos mine. The representative of the soviet in New York had endeavoured to induce him to try their asbestos. The quality of it was known to be good. Finally he said: Well, you may send us a quotation. And they sent him a quotation, which was exactly half the price he had been paying before. He was therefore compelled by the very nature of things in these difficult times to purchase that asbestos. The Canadian mine was closed down; the asbestos was acquired from Russia, and warehouses were established in which quantities were stored to meet any possible demand that might arise in connection with the business of which this gentleman was president. So we asked that, with respect to those articles of commerce, those commodities of trade in relation to which with state aid or under state control there was unfair competition, steps should be taken to enable the executive government to control such unfair competition. Finally there was introduced into the agreement the provision which will be found at the end of it, article 21:
This agreement is made on the express condition that, if either government is satisfied that any preferences hereby granted in respect of any particular class of commodities are likely to be frustrated in whole or in part by reason of the creation or maintenance directly or indirectly of prices for such class of commodities through state action on the part of any foreign country, that government hereby declares that it will exercise the powers which it now has or will heTeafter take to prohibit the entry from such foreign country directly
or indirectly of such commodities into its country for such time as may be necessary to make effective and to maintain the preferences hereby granted by it.
In other words, putting it shortly, we provided that the preferences which are set forth in the agreement should not be nullified or frustrated by reason of unfair competition under state control, and that if either government directed the attention of the other to such fact then the government whose attention was directed to that fact would take appropriate measures to prohibit for such time as might be desirable the importation into its country of this commodity or article.
