speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
not expected to ask that form of question in this house; for he knows perfectly well that no one is in a position to say whether the mine is opened up yet or not. I have not inquired, but I shall be glad to give him the address of the gentleman to whom he may write for information if he so desires.
Now let me go a step further in respect to that. Not only has that happened, but it will be recalled that a trading agreement was entered into between Great Britain and the Russian Soviet. That trading agreement is in the form of a protocol to the treaty that was to be made, and the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson signed the agreement on behalf of the British government. Owing to the long delay in negotiating the treaty of commerce the protocol was provided; it contained a provision that notice terminating it might be given, and in accordance with the agreement arrived at in Ottawa the British government has given the necessary notice. My memory is that at the end of six months that agreement will lapse by reason of the notice thus given. It will then, of course, as the British government have said, be competent for them to negotiate a fresh treaty or protocol with respect to trade with Russia. There never has been a prohibition of trade with Russia, either in Canada or in Great Britain. I directed attention the other day to the fact that we had an agreement with Russia under which quasi-diplomatic relations were maintained between the two countries. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition gave notice terminating diplomatic relations at about the same time notice was given by Great Britain after a raid had been made upon the Arcos building which housed the Russian representatives. We gave notice terminating our diplomatic relations with
950	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Russia, but we did not terminate our commercial relations. Russia has been buying from us, and, in a smaller way, we have bought some few commodities from Russia. When this government came into power, however, representations were made to the effect that competition was most unfair with regard to many articles, and we took power to pass an order in council prohibiting the importation into this country from Russia of commodities that might be indicated or goods that might be specified. In accordance with the power thus conferred on the government an order in council was passed that did prohibit the importation into this jountry of anthracite coal and several other articles including furs, though that later was amended to mean furs not raw but partly fabricated, and it included pulpwood as well.
Let us see the reason for that action. Apart altogether from the unfair competition, any person passing down the St. Lawrence river, as I did, might have seen ships laden with pulpwood from Russia, which was being sold in Canada at a price that bore no relation to the cost of production. That was clear. Those who saw the hard coal that came to this country realized that the price at which it was being offered at the start would have had the effect of entirely destroying the trade with Great Britain, which we were endeavouring to foster, and to some extent the trade with the United States. We conceived it to be our duty on the facts before us, to pass the order in council which we did pass and which had the effect of prohibiting the importation into this country of the articles specified.
I think this may be an appropriate time to make an observation with regard to oil, because more than one hon. member opposite has referred to that question. While an investigation is still under way with respect to oil, I will only say this: Last spring representatives of a large industrial concern in this country asked the government to agree to the exchange of aluminum for hard coal. We told them we did not propose to change the terms of the order in council that prohibited the importation of hard coal from Russia, for two reasons. Apart altogether from the unfair competition and the conditions under which the coal was mined and shipped, there was one other factor. We had been endeavouring to assist the Welsh hard coal industry, which could survive as far as Canada was concerned only if that prohibition was maintained. Therefore we clearly and

emphatically told these interests that we could not agree to any such arrangement.
But there were items not covered by the embargo, and negotiations were entered into -I am bound to say they were not communicated to me until they had been completed, for reasons that are obvious-by w'hich petroleum products were to be exchanged for aluminum. The petroleum products that came to Montreal in a Danish ship-not a Russian ship-were a mixture of crude oil, fuel oil and gasoline. An analysis would indicate that the gasoline had been through cracking coils, in other words, had been manufactured or refined by the latest and best methods known, and then mixed with a small quantity of fuel oil and crude petroleum to bring it up to the requisite specific gravity to come within the terms of our tariff item and enable it to be classified as crude oil not in its natural state. Our policy in this country has been, since we have had no substantial quantity of crude oil produced here, to permit it to find access to our markets free of duty. Crude oil not in its natural state, that is, synthetic crude built up from a mixture of petroleum products, has had to pay a duty of three-tenths of a cent, one-sixth of a cent, and so on, per gallon. When it became apparent that this product was a mixture of refined gasoline, crude petroleum and fuel oil, w7hich is crude petroleum from which the lighter and more volatile substances have been taken, and which has a very considerable weight, it became clear that these substances had been blended for the purpose of creating the requisite specific gravity to enable the mixture to come within that item in the tariff which describes it as crude oil not in its natural state.
The matter then resolved itself into a determination, which the Department of National Revenue is carrying on, of how that oil should be classified. But there was still another question, that of fair or unfair competition. We had to consider whether or not the introduction into this country, under the conditions I have mentioned, of quantities of so called crude oil at prices which, while comparable with the prices of crude oil imported from the United States or South America, were not comparable, it is alleged, with the prices of the different ingredients making up that product, constituted unfair competition. In other words, if the product was something from which gasoline could be obtained merely by rectification, without requiring to be refined, that condition would constitute unfair competition.

United Kingdom
The only point that arises in this regard under this agreement is in connection with petroleum from the island of Trinidad. Trinidad has been producing substantial quantities of crude oil. In itself that crude oil is not of the highest quality, and the importation of petroleum products into Canada from Trinidad has meant the importation of a mixture of a partly refined product and crude and fuel oils, something like the Russian product. Trinidad oil has a preference under the agreement into which we have entered, and the question was whether or not the importation of this product from Russia constituted unfair competition within the terms of article 21, which I have just read. That matter is still under consideration and advisement, and the government depends for its ultimate decision upon those facts which are capable of exact determination ibut which as yet have not been determined. If, as a result of the exact determination of those questions, it becomes apparent that this imported petroleum product, call it what you may, is calculated to frustrate the operation of the agreement as it now stands with regard to the island of Trinidad, then there will be *,n embargo against the importation of that oil into Canada.
The next provision to which I direct attention is this:	Having received the benefits to
which I have referred-and I use that word "benefits" despite the fact that seme objection has been taken to it and to the word "concessions"-under the agreement, we undertook to pass legislation giving effect to the provisions contained in schedule E attached to the agreement. When the agreements were concluded they were not published to the world in so far as tariff changes were concerned, except where they w'ere of a character that would not in any sense involve forestalling or the making of purchases in anticipation of the enactment of the legislation. Schedule E was not published. It was first published when it was made known to this house, and immediately upon being made known to this house the proper resolutions were moved in order that it might become part of the tariff structure and that forestalling cr the anticipation of its provisions in the way of purchases could be prevented.
These tariff schedules which we have submitted to the house involve as well as schedule E to this agreement the other tariff provisions with respect to South Africa and the other British dominions. It is clear that in stating the articles with respect to w'hich we were willing to make changes we did so in general terms, and I think my right hon. friend will realize that it became essential to
carry into our tariff structure the changes brought about by reason of the agreement. And so the Minister of Finance has in his hands the schedules in the ways and means committee for the purpose of incorporating into our tariff structure the changes which we agreed to make in the agreement with the United Kingdom and the other dominions.
It is perfectly true we bound ourselves for five years to maintain in a general way the tariff structure that I have mentioned; it is perfectly true that changes may be made from time to time. The margin is to be preserved. Rut there is one other point to which I desire to direct attention and it is this. We realize that in this changing world, having made the arrangements we have and which we believe are beneficial to this dominion, it was desirable also to anticipate the possibilities of changes being made, and so in order that there might be no doubt that the general rule that governs with respect to contracts should prevail, in article 23 we have stipulated that in the event of circumstances arising which, in the judgment of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom or of His Majesty's government in Canada, as the case may be, necessitate a variation in the terms of the agreement, the proposal to vary these terms shall form the subject of consultation between the two governments. In other words, dealing as we were with our own people and making arrangements having regard to the depressed conditions that exist in the world and the universal character of the depression, but which arrangements two years from now, to use the language of one hon. gentleman opposite, it might be desirable to change, we have contemplated that the two governments should consult for the purpose of arriving at any changes that may be desired.
Sir, I am not oblivious of the criticisms that were made -when the resolution was before the house, that these tariff reductions do not go far enough. I suspect that most Canadians realize, judging from the communications I receive, and the statements I hear, that after all the statesmen from the United Kingdom might fairly be regarded as alive to their own interests and capable of determining to what extent the tariffs should be reduced to permit of their making the concessions they have made to us. That would seem to me to be axiomatic, but apparently I am wrong, for I have listened day after day to hon. gentlemen complaining that sufficient concessions have not been granted to the United Kingdom. Who is the best judge of that-we or they? Their House of Commons has adopted this agreement; I believe it is adopted today in the
952	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Lords. Their house met on the 18th day of October and we met twelve days before that. Those who will take the trouble to read Hansard and analyze the speeches that have been made will realize how great has been the concern of the average member for the taxpayer in Great Britain and how little has been his concern for Canadians. They will realize the extent to which he has been crying and weeping over the taxation of food which he is not going to pay, his commiseration with the poor man in England, his concern for him. But are not British statesmen capable of seeing to that? Did the parliament of Great Britain vote down by one of the greatest majorities in its history the amendment that dealt with that very feature, or did it not? If the press Reports are to be relied upon, the parliament of Great Britain gave no uncertain answer to that issue, because they knew that there would be no increase in the tax on food. They knew that unless the British miller desired to buy his grain from some other than a British country there was no tax payable, but that if he desired to buy from a foreigner he would pay the tax. That is his business, not ours. And the British House of Commons adopted that view without difficulty.
It has also been said that, with respect to textiles, there should have been a much greater reduction in tariffs. I explained that specific duties had been reduced 33^ per cent in one case and 25 per cent in the other, and the hostile press complained and carried articles showing how little it meant. Did it ever occur to this house that so far as we are concerned the law of the country, enacted as it is in tariff legislation, provided for these imposts in order that there might not be a collapse of industry in a period of world depression such as we have never seen heretofore? Will anyone say, in looking at the work that has been done by the textile industry in Canada during the last two years, in affording employment, that its rate of reward has been incommensurate with the risk? Who will say that? Will anyone say that their profits have been unfair or unreasonable? Does anyone want to see the industry killed? Judging by some speeches that have been made on the opposite side, some hon. gentlemen apparently desire that the industry should be destroyed, notwithstanding that for every dollar made, 12 cents goes to the exchequer of the country. And if we are to have, as has been said, an increase in income tax for the purpose of providing revenue with the aid of the printing press, then of course it follows clearly that if there are no profits there is no revenue; and no one who has studied the reports of any textile 	Ji , T
industry in Canada, whether it be cotton, wool or silk, will say that these profits have been extravagant during the last two years.
This I say: Had we not passed the legislation we did in 1930, there would have been no textile industry operating in Canada today
not any. And what is more, there is not a thoughtful observer, not an economist, not an analyst who does not say that this is so- not one. Why? During the very discussions that took place during this conference, when we were talking about textiles, on the very day when the conversations opened in connection with cottons, there came into my hands a statement to the effect that before a judge of the chancery division in London a motion had been made to reduce the capital of one of the greatest cotton industries in Lancashire by £4,000,000-not dollars-because their trading loss had been £3,000,000-their trading loss! And we are asked to say that the proper thing to do in a country such as this is to allow concerns that are making a trading loss to destroy Canadian enterprises. That is what we are asked to do. Take the condition of the woollen industry in this country when we came into office. Will any man say that as a result of the few years that preceded 1930 the effect was not to destroy that industry?
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was; and what is
more, no man knows it better than the exMinister of Trade and Commerce, because the facts and figures are on file this very day in the office which he formerly occupied. Industries which today are flourishing in little communities in Ontario, giving employment to fifty or a hundred people, were closed down when we came in. Moreover, the entire industry was threatened with insolvency. That is the position. We saved the industry by the action we took. We saved the cotton industry of this country, we maintained the silk industry, and of every dollar they have made during the last two years from ten to twelve per cent has been paid into the Canadian exchequer.
We were confronted with competition of a character such as this country has never seen or known of before. Were we to lie down to it? Were we to see the industry destroyed? Were we to see our country grovelling in the dust and then stand with pride on the street corner and say: Look at what has been done to these men with money whom we have destroyed. Who are the people who own these industries? Look at the share registers of the cotton companies, the woollen mills or the silk mills, and find out who they are.

United Kingdom
Vou will find there are many widows and orphans and other people who have believed in the integrity of our industry and have invested their money therein. They believed the return would be certain, but they have seen that return lessened and lowered. The result has been that money has been driven out of productive industry into bonds, largely of the country; the money has been taken out of industrial development and put into sources which will make the investment sure.
When we were faced with this situation in the preparation of these agreements we had to say to ourselves:	In these days of unfair
competition, in these days of world-wide depression, in these days when it is better, as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) has said, to choose to give employment to Canadians rather than to those who live in Czechoslovakia or any other country, we cannot make slashing reductions in the tariff without imperilling the very industrial fabric of this country built up during the last half century. I am not saying that if I had to determine whether or not some of these industries should be built up, I would build them up; I say frankly to this house, as I have said before, if I had to decide whether some of the industries in this country should or should not be here, I would say they should have never been here. But they are here, we have assisted in their maintenance and we are now confronted with a situation where we have to determine whether or not we will make such a slashing of our tariff in the concessions granted to the United Kingdom as might imperil our industrial fabric.
I said quite frankly to the British representatives: We will make the reductions I have mentioned, then we will afford you at the appropriate time an opportunity of appearing before the tariff board to present your case and to ascertain whether or not the contentions put forward by our people are well founded. This would apply also to the matter of wages. For instance, I heard yesterday of a wage of forty-five shillings being paid in an engineering trade, just one-half the rate being paid in this country.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When the house rose I was pointing out that the tariff legislation enacted by this government in 1930 and 1931 was based not upon the desire to afford protection; for those who will look at the debates of that day will realize that in presenting the
tariff changes I pointed out that they were presented, not for protection, but to afford Canadian enterprise and industry an equality of opportunity with those who were pressing them to the wall. The legislation of that time was enacted for the purpose of affording that opportunity to Canadian enterprise and industry which we believed then and which we still believe its importance demanded.
May I point out further that last year we made provision for the appointment of a tariff board. It became apparent to me, after carefully considering the matter, that owing to the difficulty that would be experienced by any body of men meeting together in conference to determine what should constitute reasonable and fair opportunity for competition, it would be almost impossible for an agreement to be arrived at, and rather than make striking changes in the tariff we provided that:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake forthwith to constitute the tariff board for which provision is made in the Tariff Board Act, 1931.
The principle upon which that tariff board will act, apart from what is declared in the statute itself, is contained in article 11, which reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that during the currency of this agreement the tariff shall be based on the principle that protective duties shall not exceed such a level as will give United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition on the basis of the relative cost of economical and efficient production, provided that in the application of such principle special consideration shall be given to the case of industries not fully established.
That is a recognition of the doctrine of John Stuart Mill, and at the same time it is a fair and complete statement of what we conceive should be the principles that govern tariffs in this country, namely, that our own people should be afforded at least an equal opportunity with those who produce outside this country to compete for the home market as well as for their share of the markets abroad.
Then we provided that the findings of the tariff board, this fact finding body, should be laid before parliament so that the force of public opinion, for what it might be worth, would always be available for the purpose of making clear just what the situation was as disclosed by the report, and we provided that such action would be taken as the character of the report warranted.
We further agreed that we would not increase existing duties on United Kingdom goods until after an investigation and report by the board in accordance with the facts as found by that body, and further that United
954	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Kingdom producers should have an opportunity of presenting their case to the tariff board.
During the course of the debate attention was directed to the fact that on a previous occasion I had asked the house why it was that those who lived outside of this country were permitted to come in and present their case to the tariff board. Under the circumstances that then existed I think that was the view entertained by many members on both sides of the house. Now, having established a board and having made it part of an international agreement, the agreement between the United Kingdom and ourselves, we have provided that inasmuch as it is to find the facts upon which action may be based, the fullest opportunity should be afforded to the other party to the agreement to present a case in support of any views which may be in the mind of the producers of the United Kingdom as to the necessity for any tariff we may have imposed.
The paragraphs relating to administration, some have said, are a reflection upon the administration of the Customs department of this country. I think that that has been amply dealt with, and I shall not do more than say this:	When Great Britain went
off the gold standard this country was confronted with the greatest crisis of its economic history. We had a pound which was valued for the purpose of the purchase of merchandise at a price that was not more than two-thirds of its par value. The customs tariffs of this country had been predicated upon a pound of the value of $4.86f. Now if there was any adequacy in the tariffs as passed, it follows that with the depreciation of the pound to the extent to which it had depreciated there was a wholly inadequate provision in our tariffs to afford an equality of opportunity to Canadian producers. So we had recourse to the provisions of the statute which enabled us to value for duty purposes imports coming into t-his countiy. We had also in our statute a further provision with respect to what was called the dumping currency duty.
Let me make clear to the house just what has been done. The pound had a par value of $4.86f. Immediately Great Britain went off the gold pound it was believed that there would be a rapid rise in commodity prices and in wages. I was waited upon by representatives of large importing houses who sought relief, under the provisions of our statute giving us power to impose dumping duties on depreciated currency, from what they believed would be a very difficult situation. I ventured to believe at that time, and so

expressed myself, that within a reasonable time a ten per cent increase in commodity prices would be all that would happen. I do not know that I had any very great reason for making that observation. But at any rate, deducting 48 cents from $4.86, leaves roughly $4.38, and we finally fixed $4.40 as the value of the pound for the purpose of dealing with it under the statute. It transpired, for some strange reason which economists have not been able to explain, or anyone else up to this moment, that instead of commodity prices and wages rising rapidly in Great Britain as expected, the rise was much slower, and has been and still is. The board of trade figures indicate that the increased value of commodities and of wages averages 8.8 per cent There has been a great decrease in wages, but the average figure furnished by the board of trade with respect to the rise in commodity values was only 8.8 per cent. Now we had based our figures on practically a ten per cent appreciation in commodity value. The dumping duty is the difference between the actual value of the pound, that is its value on the exchanges as fixed between New York and London from day to day, and $4.40. That is to say, if the average value of the pound for a period of fifteen days has been $3.80, the. difference between that and $4.40 fixed the currency dumping duty, which would be 60 cents on the pound. The house will see that the effect of that is that we have been more than fair; for having computed and estimated our duties on the basis of the par value of the pound, we have by arbitrary action reduced its value to $4.40, and provided that instead of the measure of relief that would be afforded by the difference between say an average of $3.80 and $4.86, the difference shall be computed between $3.80 and $4.40. As a matter of fact, the representatives of the British producers in this country expressed the view that it was not an unfair arrangement; that is, that having made our computations and arranged our fiscal system on a basis of the par value of the pound, we arbitrarily reduced it to $4.40, believing that the effect of England going off the gold standard would be to raise commodity values by substantially ten per cent.
We had that factor to deal with, and it is a factor that is still with us. I wonder if hon. gentlemen realize that in some instances the effect of the depreciation of the pound in this country is to render nugatory any provisions that there are in the tariff ait all. In some cases there is practically no tariff if you have regard to just the ordinary exchange value of

United Kingdom
the pound. If in availing ourselves of the provisions of our statutes we are censurable for having done what we could to maintain the industrial and commercial structure of this country, then, of course, I can understand it. If, on the other hand, the government is not to be censured for availing itself of the provisions of a law designed to meet just such an emergency as that which has arisen, I think we are entitled to commendation. We have further provided that when conditions warrant it we will take the necessary action so far as these dumping duties are concerned, and we have protected of course the Canada-West Indies agreement of 1925 which has still some five years to run. This parliament and this government-although it is not the same parliament, and not the same government-we felt were bound in honour to protect the treaty obligation of this dominion extended to the West Indies, and we have made provision for it accordingly.
The provision with respect to the continuance of the agreement will be found in article 22. It is to last for five years, and then it must be terminated 'by six months notice after that time. To-night I am not going to repeat the argument I have already adduced as to why in the opinion of those well able to form an opinion, apart altogether from the government itself, the period of five years is not too long a time within which to test the efficacy of an agreement of this kind. In fact, when dealing with a purely empire agreement it might have been successfully contended that a longer time was desirable. If, for instance, in negotiating with the West Indies we believed it desirable to have a twelve year term, because it. was a family agreement, one might readily understand why in dealing with the mother country a five years term did not seem unreasonable. The same might be said as to the circumstances under which the agreement will continue in force until six months' notice has been given. At this moment I do not purpose to do more than to indicate, as I have already done, why the agreement was made and why it appears in its present terms.
Only yesterday my attention was directed to a great headline in a British newspaper stating that " Bennett and his lumber friends " dictate the policy of the United Kingdom. There are those in this country who, in the debate which took place upon the resolution -and possibly I am not strictly within the rules of the house in making this statement- contended that John Bull, and I am using the language of one of the hon. members opposite, has dictated to us what we should do. I use
these two illustrations because they indicate extraordinary points of view. In fact the right hon. gentleman who leads the apposition suggested that pressure had been used, and wanted to know whether or not the agreement had been signed under compulsion, or otherwise. It does seem to me that such a suggestion is foreign to the whole theory and practice of a conference, but I will not do more than say that the representatives of this empire convened in this city of Ottawa, discussed their difficulties, pointed out their desire to extend trade. We in particular voiced a wish to increase our export trade. As a result of that conference arrangements were made which were accepted by all. Those agreements are evidenced by our signatures, not to single agreements but to bilateral agreements whereby each community determined what was in its best interest. In the mutual interests of all the agreements were executed.
The agreement before the house is that between the United Kingdom and Canada, and the factors which influenced us in arriving at the conclusions I have indicated have, I think, been sufficiently set forth in the debate which has already taken place, and in my remarks this afternoon. I shall not longer delay the proceedings of the house, except to point out that in article 11 the word "shall" was in the original draft as printed. But by arrangement between the two governments, and in accordance with provisions contained in the agreement itself, the word "shall" has been changed to "may", and so appeals in the bill before the house.
In schedule E, item 210, in respect of "nitrate of soda or cubic nitre n.o.p." a new item 210e has been added, as follows:
210e. Nitrate of soda or cubic nitre imported by manufacturers of explosives for use exclusively in the manufacture of explosives in their own factories: free; free; free.
Although item 210 as set forth in the agreement carries the rates of free, 15 per cent and 20 per cent, the two governments, after consultation, have satisfied themselves that the United Kingdom is not in a position at the moment to supply Canadian requirements of nitrate of soda. But when it is in a position to satisfy Canadian requirements for all purposes the rate of duty will be as set forth in item 210.
Then, I direct the attention of the house to schedule F of the agreement, Canadian tariff item 784, "crude peanut oil, for refining for edible purposes, used as materials in Canadian manufactures." That item has been deleted entirely from the schedule. The de-
956	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
cision was made after consultation with the two governments affected. The item in question came into the tariff schedule under, shall I say, accidental circumstances, and as soon as it was brought to the attention of the two governments it was deleted. In the Ottawa Agreements Act, the title of the bill which passed the British House of Commons on November 3, the changes to which I have referred, in so far as they affect the agreement with the United Kingdom, have been made.
Without endeavouring to gloss over difficulties, to magnify advantages or to minimize disadvantages, I have ventured this afternoon and this evening to retrace part of the ground that has already been covered in previous discussions. I do so on second reading of the bill because schedule E set out in the bill is the only statement of the general principles with respect to the items now found in the ways and means resolutions in the hands of the Minister of Finance. He is prepared with his resolutions to afford every possible information to the house with respect to the volume of trade which may be affected, and the manner in which it may be brought about. Of course he will have to have the assistance of his technical officers. If hon. members opposite desire, as is their right, to record their vote against the second reading of this measure, I suggest that having done that the bill be passed with as much expedition as possible to its third reading, and that the ways and means resolutions be then taken up, because they cover not only those items set forth in schedule E of this agreement, but they also embody, in accordance with the provisions of our tariff, all the other items concerning tariffs that are dealt with in the other agreements with which reference has been made. If with the votes and proceedings before them, setting out fully the existing rates and the proposed rates in terms of the tariff legislation of the country, hon. members make such inquiries as they deem necessary, they can more fully appreciate and understand the tariff provisions of the agreements; and the Minister of Finance, as I have said, is in a position then to afford every possible opportunity for discussion of any or all of the items, as may be desired.
I have trespassed longer than I had intended upon the time of the house. I did so, however, because there have been some misconceptions which should be cleared up, and there were others which I thought should be exposed as being wholly unworthy of support. With confidence I commend the agreement to

the house as worthy at least of a trial during the period of time that is fixed; for it is my belief that within the four corners of this and the other agreements that have been submitted to this parliament lies the best insurance we can have of the return of that stable prosperity which it is the earnest desire of us all to see in this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING:
speechtext:
.Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, since the introduction into this house of the resolution respecting the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, we have had the opportunity of listening to three addresses of not inconsiderable length by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) with reference to that agreement. The first was at the time of introducing the resolution on which the bill before the house at the moment is based; the second was the address delivered on Thursday evening last in closing the debate which took place on the resolution; and the third is the address to which we have just listened on the second reading.
With respect to the address which the Prime Minister has given the house today, there are marked contrasts with his previous utterances; there is also a marked similarity.
More light and less heat.

With respect to the contrasts, may I say that my right hon. friend's first address might, I think, have been described as very 'largely provocative. It was to some extent explanatory, but very largely provocative. His address on Thursday evening last was very largely denunciatory. The speech to which we have listened this aftemon and evening has been mostly explanatory and argumentative. May I say that I think it would have been more befitting one who presided over the great conference, and who hopes to have his name associated with legislation which will result *therefrom, had he, in his previous discussions and throughout this debate, adopted somewhat more the tone which he has adopted this evening.
May I, Mr. Speaker, say at once that I wish to take very strong exception to our being asked to pass the second reading of this bill without having had any opportunity of discussing in detail the several items in the tariff schedule which form a part of the bill, and which, as a matter of fact, constitute its main feature from the Canadian point of view. It is with reference to the Prime Minister's failure to make any reference to this side of

United Kingdom
the so-called bargain that I find the similarity in all the speeches he has made. In all of them he has dwelt at very considerable length upon what Great Britain proposes to give to Canada by way of what he terms concessions. He has said practically nothing with respect to the significance to Canada of the tariff changes proposed in the schedule attached to the agreement. These tariff items, had they been few in number and their significance easily determined, might have permitted of slight reference and treatment. But, as hon. members know, this schedule of tariff changes amounts to a revision of the Canadian tariff more extensive, certainly more serious, than possibly any other revision that has been made in the Canadian tariff since we have had a tariff. It is quite possible to compare in extent the present revision with the one by Mr. Fielding in 1907, and to some extent with the changes made at the time of the Dunning budget. It is at least comparable in extent with those great changes. It has this feature in addition, that it not only purports to make changes in the Canadian tariff with respect to Canadian tariffs peculiarly, but, as the Prime Minister himself has said, it is part of a new imperial policy, an imperial tariff policy. We are beginning an innovation in tariff affairs and in imperial affairs, by being asked to legislate on an imperial tariff. Notwithstanding this, we have had no opportunity whatever of discussing in detail the several items in the schedule: a schedule, may I point out further, which raises the tariff of Canada to heights considerably above the inordinate heights it had reached at the time the conference was held. It goes a step further. Not only does it raise the tariff to these greater heights, but it aims at doing something which has not been attempted before in any perceptible way; it aims at making a permanent tariff by rendering it impossible for this House of Commons over a period of years to reduce duties beyond a certain level. That Mr. Speaker, is a very great departure, and I submit that in those circumstances this House of Commons should have had, and ought still to have before it is asked to approve this agreement, full opportunity of discussing all these tariff items in detail. Tariff items are matters of taxation, and the control of taxation is the peculiar prerogative of the House of Commons. It is the oldest of the established rights of the commons to supervise all matters that pertain to taxation, and it is that right which at the present time we are being denied.
Now the Prime Minister has given to the house as a reason for proceeding as he does, that he is following the procedure which is
customary with respect to the introduction of tariff bills. He says that when the Minister of Finance brings in his budget, the new duties go into effect immediately. That is quite correct, but may I point out what takes place when the Minister of Finance introduces his budget? After introducing his budget the Minister of Finance presents to the committee of ways and means resolutions which embody all the changes that it is proposed to make in the tariff, and those resolutions are discussed in detail in committee of ways and means before any bill purporting to implement those changes is introduced. After the House of Commons has exercised to the full its right to discuss in detail all the proposed tariff changes which the Minister of Finance embodies in his budget, the Minister of Finance introduces a bill to confirm the proposed items of the tariff in the light of all the suggestions or modifications that may have been made.

That is precisely what
we are doing here.
We are not in committee, as the Prime Minister said.

Perhaps the
Minister of Trade and Commerce will permit me to say that during the time the Prime Minister spoke this afternoon and evening he was not interrupted by anyone, let alone anyone on the front benches. I think the same was true of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he was speaking. I ask, Mr. Speaker, that I be allowed the same opportunity to express the Liberal point of view in regard to this agreement as we accorded to hon. gentlemen opposite to express their view.

What about last
Thursday?

The Minister
of Trade and Commerce says that is what we are doing here. It is not what we are doing here; it is what we are told we may do after this agreement which includes the schedule of tariff changes has been approved by this House of Commons-an entirely different thing. Let me repeat, that when the Minister of Finance in connection with any tariff changes which he may introduce in a bill desires to get the approval of this house for those tariff changes, he first presents them in the form of resolutions to the house for its discussion in committee of the whole, where every item may be scrutinized, where full opportunity is given for discussion as to
958	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
the degree to which the proposed changes are likely to affect trade and like considerations, and where the amplest opportunity is given all hon. members to express themselves fully and the house to become fully seized of the significance of the changes. After that has taken place in committee of the whole house, and the resolutions have been approved, a bill is then introduced and the bill is given its first reading. It is then given second reading, and after the second reading all the items are discussed again with the possibility of amendment. After that stage has been passed the bill is given a third reading, goes to the other house and after passing through similar stages there, finally receives the royal assent. But what are we now being asked to do? The bill before us for second reading is a very short document. It has only three paragraphs; the first sets forth the short title, the last gives the government the necessary authority to carry out its provisions, and the second says that this parliament approves the agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada, which agreement embodies all these tariff changes. So we are being asked to approve all the tariff changes, which are entirely new and which affect our general tariff as against all countries as well as the preferences accorded Great Britain and the other dominions. We have to pass upon these without any knowledge of what they really are or what their effect is likely to be.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is not treating the House of Commons fairly. It is taking away from this house its oldest, most sacred and most fundamental right and duty, and it is doing that under a mere pretext and pretence. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance know that if there was the slightest desire on the part of the government to give the house an opportunity to discuss these matters, that could be done without violating any rule of the house and without altering the procedure in any particular. Before the house at the moment there are the resolutions before the committee of ways and means, which the Prime Minister says he hopes we will leave until everything else is disposed of, until after we have approved of the agreement and all that is in it. Then, he says, we can discuss these resolutions at great length. I say, Mr. Speaker, this house should be moved into committee of the whole to consider ways and means, and there we would be afforded an opportunity to discuss all the resolutions which have been presented to the house by the Minister of Finance. Then, when we have discussed these resolutions in committee and

have become fully seized of the nature of the tariff changes which are a part of this bill, let us return to the second reading of the bill and give our approval or disapproval of the agreement and the schedule of tariff changes embodied in it.
If that step is not taken-and even yet it is not too late for the government to take if-then with respect to a great inter-empire matter, with respect to perhaps the most far-reaching of all the steps that have been taken in regard to fiscal policy in the British Empire since there has been a British Empire, this House of Commons of Canada is being denied its oldest, most fundamental and most sacred right. That is, I submit, a poor way in which to try to build up any new system that is intended to make for imperial unity. I say it is a subterfuge of the worst possible kind. Under the guise of making an agreement between Canada and Great Britain with respect to trade, we are being asked to do what? We are asked not to make an agreement that is simply going to facilitate trade between Canada and different parts of the British Empire, but to make an agreement which for years to come is going to make increasingly difficult trade between Canada and the other countries of the world. That is the situation, and in the main that is the objection we have to this measure now before the house, and the wajr in which it is presented.
I want to make that very clear, Mr. Speaker. This legislation which we are being asked to approve will make increasingly difficult trade between this country and the other countries of the world. That is its primary object, and before I am through speaking this evening, I shall quote words direct from the lips of the Prime Minister himself in which he made the unmistakable declaration that the effect of this legislation would be to exclude the foreigner, and that this was the real purpose of the legislation now before us. I say that is a very serious step for a country to take, and it is doubly serious when it is taken in the dark as we are asked to take it at the present time. If for no other reason than that, I say it would be impossible for those of us who wish to respect the rights and privileges of parliament and to do our duty as representatives of the people in matters of the control of taxation and the like to think of supporting the second reading of this measure. We could not do so and maintain the traditions and rights of parliament which above all else w"e are here to maintain.
Now may I come to the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister cm Thursday evening of last week. I speak of that at once [DOT]because in that speech the Prime Minister

United Kingdom
sought to tell this house and the country what the principles of the Liberal party were with respect to matters of inter-empire trade. He undertook to tell the house what previous leaders of the Liberal party had stood for in these matters and what the policies were, and he lectured us upon not being true to our past leaders, and upon not being true to our principles. May I say to the Prime Minister that if he will confine himself to his own party and its policies, I think he will have quite enough to do. The last thing we would expect from the leader of the Commons and the Prime Minister of the country, let alone from the one who presided over the imperial conference, would be a deliberate misrepresentation of the position of any political party with respect to inter-empire trade since interempire trade became an actuality. And may I say that the last thing we would expect from any man would be an effort to misrepresent one who held a position second to no other in this country as the leader of a government and of a party, and to misrepresent that position when he whose memory all Canada so greatly reveres is not here to be heard on his own behalf. I am going to have something to say this evening, Mr. Speaker, about the references which have been made by the Prime Minister to the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and if the house will do me the honour of listening to a simple statement of the Liberal position as it is to be found in Liberal records, and as it is set forth in the utterances of the great Liberal leader whose name has been used so lightly by the right hon. gentleman opposite, I think they will soon discover that the right hon. Prime Minister is the last man entitled to claim, even today, to be a follower of that great leader.
What was the nature of the speech made by the Prime Minister the other evening? It reminded me of nothing quite so much as the nature of the campaign which he conducted in 1930. In all particulars the present Prime Minister ran true to form. He began by talking about the great betrayal, how leaders had been betrayed by their following, and how the following had been betrayed by its leaders. He spoke of betrayal three or four times during the course of his speech. I think we all still remember how he opened the conservative campaign in Winnipeg in 1930. In his remarks on the first night of the campaign he spoke of the great betrayal. He referred to the hon. members of the government of the day as a band of mercenaries, betraying all their principles. The following night speaking at Regina, he said the great betrayal had been
carried on for nine years; that it did not take Judas that long. That was the kind of language we heard from the present Prime Minister then the leader of the opposition, during the campaign. One can understand hearing it from him from a public platform during a political campaign, but I submit that we hardly had reason to expect it in this House of Commons from the leader of a government bringing in a great measure of fiscal reform.
How did the Prime Minister conclude his speech the other evening? He finished with a denunciation of all hon. members on this side of the house, telling them, in so many words, that they were voting not for principle, but in fear of the crack of the whip, that they stood in awe of their leader and did not dare to vote contrary to the way he voted.
Hear, hear.

Well, let the Prime Minister judge his own following in the light of those words, if he wishes so to do. May I tell him that, whatever view he may have of his own following, hon. gentlemen on this side of the house speak their own minds and stand by their own principles. What was the nature of his appeal? Exactly the same as the appeal made in 1930, when the right hon. gentleman visited different parts of the country and appealed to local prejudice of each-appealing to those who were apple growers by telling them that they needed protection for their apples; appealing to those in the mining industry on the ground that they needed protection for their industries; on the prairies appealing to the farmers by telling them that they needed and would receive something in the way of compensation for the protection he was giving to others; in the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec appealing to the dairy farmers on the necessity for protection on butter and various other commodities; to the textile and boot and shoe workers on their need for more in the way of protection; then down at the Atlantic coast appealing to the fishermen on the need of protection of the fishing industry. And so on back and forth all through the country, telling the great mass of people that, if returned to power, he would see that everyone would be supplied with w'ork-work for all; not doles, but work. This is the right hon. gentleman who speaks about betrayal, one who came into office on the promise that he would see that there would be an immediate end to work-

Oh, oh.
960	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements

An immediate end to unemployment, rather. The necessity of work for the people was so much in my mind at the moment that that word slipped in where I should have used the word "unemployment." The right hon. gentleman said that, if he were returned to power, there would be work for all; work, not doles, he said; that there would be markets for the produce of the farmers; these he would blast [DOT] for them; that there would be old age pensions for everyone at the expense of the federal government; that there would be a [DOT] highway running from the Atlantic to the Pacific; that there would be public works everywhere. And now, after more than two years in which to implement those promises, what has happened? Not one of the promises has been fulfilled, on every one of them the people of Canada have been betrayed.
The other evening the Prime Minister, before the vote was taken, made an attempt at intimidation-an effort to browbeat and intimidate hon. members of the House of Commons on this side of the house. Think of the Prime Minister of a country adopting an attitude of the kind towards hon. gentlemen in a chamber over which he presides, asking one after another-Would he dare to get up and inform his constituents that he had voted against protection on apples? Would he dare to tell his constituents that he had voted against protection on fish? Would he dare to tell his constituents that he had voted against a free market for wheat? And so on, and so on. With an appeal to local prejudice, he denounced and sought to intimidate, one after another, hon. members on this side. Well, he got his answer. Some one says 48 of a majority. Well, the Prime Minister has told hon. gentlemen opposite in so many words, inferentially if not directly, just why the majority was what it was.
The only difference that I can see in the nature of the appeal, of the other evening and that of the campaign of 1930, was that in 1930 it was Canada first. Now, we have reached another stage; it is now empire first. The right hon. gentleman speaks of " the family"; we must 'take care of "the family." The agreement with respect to the West Indies and Canada was sacred because it concerned a part of " the family." But what did the right hon. gentleman eay with regard to moneys spent in trade in the West Indies? He said, " If a dollar goes to the West Indies which ought to have been spent in Canada, it might as well have been spent in the United States." That is how mutch he cares for " the family"; and, if we are to reason by analogy,

I suppose it will be precisely the same with respect to all other parts of the empire: every dollar spent in South Africa or in New Zealand or in Australia, every dollar spent in England or in Scotland, or in any other part of the empire, which might have been spent in Canada, might, from his point of view, as well have been spent in the United States. That is his view of the sacredness of " the family "- the money if not spent in Canada, might just as well, so far as the other members of the family are concerned, have been spent in the United States.
That, I think, fairly well summarizes the attitude of the rigfct hon. gentleman the other evening. There was one thing more, however, thoroughly characteristic of him, which disclosed that he was running true to form. He was not content to rest his case on the strength of the argument, on the strength of the proposition itself, on what advantage was going to accrue from the agreement to Canada and the empire. He had to go out of his way to make one of the meanest and most contemptible of personal attacks against the leader of the opposition. I have been reading over the words of my right hon. friend and I confess I have not had much difficulty in discovering how he came to use them; they were words which, everything considered, would come very naturally to his mind. He spoke of wounded pride, wounded vanity; he talked about resentment, about anger, about spleen, about not being too exclusively in the spotlight. Well, had the right hon. gentleman desired to reveal his own mind, his own feelings, he could not have taken a better way so to do. The Prime Minister seems to think that it is impossible for any man in public life to be actuated by motives of public service and principle. These considerations do not seem to enter bis mind. It is always some personal motive, some end of vanity to be served, some end of pride, some feeling of resentment, spleen in its many forms where someone or something has in some way crossed his path and must as a consequence be destroyed. That is all he seems able to think of when he comes to meet an opponent who happens to differ from him, be it only in matters of opinion.
May I say that, as regards any personal attacks which he may wish to make upon myself, he is most welcome to continue to make them. I doubt whether he could say more about me than he has already said. If he can think of any derogatory word in the vocabulary which has escaped him, which he has not already used in regard to myself, I shall be very glad to hear it.

United Kingdom
I would add it to the collection I have already of what he has said concerning me-a collection of which I feel somewhat proud, to tell the truth, because I do not think the Prime Minister would find it necessary to resort to language of this description did he not feel that there was a good deal in the arguments which he has been called upon to meet and has been unable to meet on their merits. If he lives very long, he will come to regret many times, many of the expressions he has used, and in no respect will he regret them more than in relation to this agreement with which he hopes to have his name associated as a great measure of imperial fiscal reform.
I will not take up more time with reference to the speech made the other evening, except to observe that the rest of it falls into two parts. The first was an effort to misrepresent from beginning to end the position of the Liberal party with respect to imperial preference and, in particular, the position of its leaders, and, above all, to detract from the great name of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Xaurier.
That is not true.

Just a moment; my hon. friends will see that it is true. The other part of the speech was an endeavour to offer, or to appear to offer, some answer to arguments which were put forward from this side. It was not an answer to those arguments, as I think I shall be able to show.
In reviewing the history of the Liberal party with respect to preference, the Prime Minister began with the year 1S97. I am going to go back a year or two before that in order to give the genesis of the movement as it appears in the records of this house. I think I can show that, in the very first debate which took place in this house on the subject, there was a fundamental difference in the points of view of the two political parties with respect to the whole question of imperial preference, points of view which have been fundamentally at variance from the beginning until today, and which account for the -difference between hon. gentlemen opposite and ourselves at the present time.
I do not intend to follow the Prime Minister and say that his party has betrayed its principles. I will say that they are upholding today the principles which they enunciated in this parliament thirty and thirty-five years ago, but for which, during the course of that time, they never found it possible to get support. They would not have obtained support today had they proceeded in accordance with parliamentary methods and put before 53719-61
this House of Commons in the form of a tariff bill the changes in the tariff which they are trying to make under the subterfuge of an agreement with the old country.
In 1892, Mr. McNeill, then the hon. member for North Bruce, submitted the following resolution, which will be found on page 1555 of Hansard of April 25, 1892:
That if and when the parliament of Great Britain and Ireland admits Canadian products to the markets of the United Kingdom upon more favourable terms than it accords to the products of foreign countries, the parliament of Canada will be prepared to accord corresponding advantages by a substantial reduction in the duties it imposes upon British manufactured goods.
That was the Conservative policy with respect to preferences as originally enunciated, a policy which has been stated over and over again, and which it will be observed, is based not upon preference created by a decrease of customs duties, but upon an increase of customs duties-when the British parliament would increase its duties, then and then only something in the way of preference would be given by Canada to the mother country. That resolution was met by an amendment from the Liberal opposition, moved by the Hon. Sir Louis Davies. It reads:
Inasmuch as Great Britain admits the products of Canada into her ports free of duty, this house is of the opinion that the present scale of duties exacted on goods mainly imported from Great Britain should be reduced.
That resolution will be found on page 1623 of Hansard of April 25, 1892. There is shown the fundamental difference-a difference which ought to ibe admitted frankly and openly. Those who hold the views which hon. gentlemen opposite hold should be on that side of the house, and those who hold the views asserted by Sir Louis Davies ought to be on this side of the house. The view stated by Sir Louis Davies was that, inasmuch as we had a free market in Great Britain, inasmuch as she was our best customer-I think Great Britain was our best customer to the extent of taking five times the amount of commodities which we took from her-for those reasons, if for no other, we should be prepared to give her goods a certain preference in our markets by a reduction of our duties.
The preferences accorded from that day on took the form of a reduction of existing duties in favour of the United Kingdom and later on some of the other dominions. As I have said over and over again, until the conference of 1930, I do not believe there was one man in five hundred in Canada who ever thought of a preference being given in any

962	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
other way than by a reduction of duties, not one in five hundred who ever thought of a preference being given by increases in duty. Therein lies the difference between the protectionist point of view and the point of view of those who believe in freer trade. Because you stand for freer trade, it does not mean that in all circumstances, you favour absolute freedom of trade; it does mean, however, that, between the two extremes, there are those who believe -that it is to the interest of the consumer and of the producer in the great primary industries, and to the manufacturer as well, to have the costs of production and cost of living kept down, and that these ends can best be achieved by reducing duties and permitting more in the way of freedom of trade.
The right hon. gentleman has said that we have a great market in Great Britain for our manufactures. But -what is he doing by this very treaty? By increasing the cost of living, and by increasing the costs of production as he will by his further tariff increases, he is going to make it more difficult for the manufacturer in Canada, who may have any chance in the British market, to take advantage of that chance after his agreement has gone through.
In 1897 the Liberal government of the day introduced the policy of preference. The Prime Minister referred to this when he opened his discussion in these words:
Before I resume my seat I shall endeavour to make clear to the house just what the policy of the Liberal party has heretofore been, just what this new departure involves, and just why it has been made. This policy of imperial preference

That refers to the Liberal policy of imperial preference which was the one enunciated by Sir Louis Davies, that of reducing duties.
-or of preferential treatment of Canadian commodities in the British market-
Preferential treatment in the British market. How? By having Great Britain raise her duties; not by any exemption from existing duties, but by putting on duties where duties had not formerly existed.
-was a fundamental part of the teachings of Liberalism in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
In all his days, that was never a part of the teachings of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Sir Wilfrid Laurier never said at any time in his life that as a method preferences should1 be given by the establishment of duties where duties had not existed before. His whole aim in the matter of preference was to help to bring down duties, and to make trade freer between different parts of the empire and between the em-

pire and other parts of the world. The right hon. gentleman continued referring to Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
In 1897, he and his minister of finance, speaking for the government, introduced into the house measures which provided for the granting freely of preferences to goods from Great Britain.
A perfectly straightforward, honest statement of fact.
What they said then was: What we give, we give freely,-
Still quite honest and straightforward-
-without compensation, without hope of benefit. No, not without hope of benefit. True, not benefit described in words, but the latent hope that some day the British people, realizing the great concessions that Canada had granted, would give to this country in turn the benefits it had bestowed upon them.
When Sir Wilfrid Laurier made his statement, he made it perfectly clear that Canada was doing what she did because she regarded Great Britain as her best customer; because she believed in keeping down the cost of living and the cost of production in the great basic and other industries of the country; and because she believed that exports could be paid for only by imports. She believed that if vessels were to travel to and fro between this country and the old land, they would have to be laden both ways, or the cost of transportation would be greatly increased. Hon. gentlemen talk as though trade was an exchange by which one party or the other was bound to lose. That is not the point of view which Liberals hold in the matter of trade. They hold that without mutual advantage there would be no exchange of commodities at all. On this question Canada's position has repeatedly been made clear, and I do not see any reason why it should be changed.
When our preferential tariff was first adopted (1897-8), the Conservative party in parliament opposed it and held that preferences should be mutual-that Canada should not make any tariff concession to Great Britain without receiving a corresponding preference on Canadian products. I will undertake that there is not a syllable on our side of the treaty that is inconsistent with the soundest principles of free trade. What are the facts specifically in regard to the treaty? They will be found at page 23 of volume 2:
France engaged to reduce duties and remove prohibitions on a long list of articles of British production and export, iron the most important, -"the daily bread of all industries," as Cobden called it. England engaged immediately to abolish all duties upon all manufactured articles at her ports, and to reduce the duties on wine and brandy. The English reductions and abolitions extended beyond France to the commodities of all countries alike. Mr. Gladstone called 1860 the last of the cardinal and organic years of emancipatory fiscal legislation; it ended a series of which the four earlier terms had been reached in 1842, in 1845, in 1846, and 1853. With the French treaty, he used to say, the movement in favour of free trade reached its zenith.
With that treaty the movement in favour of freedom of trade reached its zenith. But with this agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom the movement in favour of high protection reaches its zenith. We were 53719-62
told last night by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryclcman) that under the agreement the government was reducing the duties on spirits and cigarettes, and was going to lose on spirits alone some $8,000,000 or more of revenue; but the Minister of National Revenue could not tell us about any revenue the government was going to lose on anything affecting the food or clothing or shelter of the great mass of the people of this country.
I come now to the inimical effect of the agreement upon our foreign trade. It constitutes the very crux of the whole situation. I ask hon. members to listen to these words, and to carry them in their minds for the rest of their lives as representing what this particular agreement seeks to accomplish. The Prime Minister made the statement very clearly on Thursday evening last. I shall read his words from the report of his speech as it will be found in Hansard. Dealing with criticisms from this side, he said:
Another says that we have closed the doors of the world's markets, that we have shut out the foreigner. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that that was one of the first things he was going to do if he got the British preference, and that is the one thing we have done.
Think of that, Mr. Speaker! We are going to close the doors of the world's markets. We have shut out the foreigner. Then to shelter himself the Prime Minister seeks to get under the aegis of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and dares to say that Sir Wilfrid Laurier sought to shut out the foreigner-
Shame!

-Sir Wilfrid
Laurier, who after fifteen years of office went down to defeat on a great reciprocal trade agreement, the aim of which was to make possible more in the way of freedom of trade with a great neighbouring country! Yet the Prime Minister of Canada would have this house and the country believe that Laurier sought to shut out the foreigner! Well, Sir Wilfrid's life and record speaks for itself. There is nothing that the present Prime Minister of Canada can ever say that will add one iota to or detract one iota from the great name and fame of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I strongly repudiate the statement or the suggestion that Sir Wilfrid at any time in respect of any measure sought to make trade more difficult between this and other countries, let alone to close the doors of the world's markets or shut out the foreigner from ours. The Prime Minister says "hear, hear," to that remark-nations outside are to pay tribute for the privilege of trading within the British empire, and we have closed the door against the foreigner. Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope the business men of this country, the manufacturers and producers, the exporters and importers, of this country, as well as the consumers, will appreciate to the full what that statement means.
The Prime Minister says that the policy is only a beginning. This is a new fiscal policy; it affects not only Canada but all parts of the British empire. What is its declared purpose? To shut out the foreigner. That is pretty serious. It is bad enough when one considers the effect on Canada alone of an attempt of the kind, but when one considers what the effect is going to be in the direction of possible retaliation by other nations, then and then only will we have a true perspective of its significance. When the effect of this policy on Canada's trade is seen, her trade with the orient, her trade with South America, her trade with Europe, her trade across the oceans of the world; when the effect upon our trade with the nations of the world is seen once they learn that the parliament of Canada has deliberately sought to shut them out of the markets of Canada; then I say that, if at that time, the present Prime Minister of Canada should be still in power there will be such an uproar from the people of this country that he will be obliged to vacate his office

I go a step further, and I say that we in this parliament had better think very carefully before we give up our national policies for any imperial policies which involve us along with other parts of the British empire in economic war. Economic war at a time such as the present will lead inevitably to hostilities between nations of the direst and most extreme kind. When we speak of the seriousness of a situation such as this the Prime Minister only laughs.
The Prime Minister claims that he has created an economic unit out of the British Empire, that he has made of the British Empire, through this arrangement, a great consolidation which is to shut out the foreigner and cause him to pay tribute in order to trade with any of its parts. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, I hope those living on the Pacific and those in the cities of the Atlantic coast will consider what this is going to mean to their ports. I hope those engaged in transportation, whether by land or by sea, will appreciate what this will mean to their enterprises as it still further adversely affects the trade of this country. I hope that the hundreds of thousands who are suffering in this country today because trade is so completely strangled and paralyzed will realize what it means when the Prime Minister of Canada says that the legislation he is passing through this house will make trade even more impossible than it is at present.
The implications of this agreement go far beyond any mere question of trade, far beyond anything in the nature merely of an economic issue. It affects the whole political future of this country and of the British Empire. It is a complete reversal of that for which, during the last few decades men of all parties, but more particularly members of the Liberal party, have striven in the evolution of the empire. At the diamond jubilee of Queen Victoria, Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier proclaimed in London that the future of the British Empire would be that of "a galaxy of nations," with each dominion enjoying full nationhood. For this he was proclaimed a separatist but his vision was clear and true. As a great political seer; he foresaw the inevitable trend if the empire were to endure. He pioneered the way in that development, and the day has come when even British statesmen have had to acknowledge Sir Wilfrid's foresight and leadership in the evolution of the commonwealth of nations as the empire is now more frequently described. The British Empire as a community of autonomous nations has found its legislative imprimatur in the Statute of Westminster which was passed

United Kingdom
within the year. But now, when this evolution has reached the point where we have a great community of free nations, so acknowledged by a statute of the British parliament, these gentlemen tell us that the bond of empire, which up till then was a political bond, has ceased to exist, and that we must seek to create in its stead some economic bond or tie which will serve to keep the general parts of the empire united and bring it to the form of a consolidated empire such as they have been seeking all along to bring about. The Apologia of an Imperialist, from which the Prime Minister has quoted, contains the record of forty years of endeavour on the part of the Tories of Great Britain and other parts of the empire to bring about an empire which would be in the nature of a great political and economic unit. They have failed to make it into a political unit; now they are striving to achieve the same end by making it into an economic unit, in which there will be imperial pollicies instead of national policies, and affairs of which apparently are to be managed by a cabinet of the combined executives of the different parts of the empire.
The Prime Minister apparently is unable to understand my reference to national sovereignty. Perhaps he has not seen a book but recently published by Mr. Berriedale Keith, the highest authority on the constitutional development of the British Empire, in which the author describes the evolution of the dominions from colonies to self-governing communities, and the evolution of the dominions from self government to national sovereignty. Now that we have achieved national sovereignty, hon. gentlemen like the Prime Minister are not satisfied. They are becoming restive, they want something which they believe to be greater still, albeit it is a reversion to a past and more dangerous order. By means of Imperial policies, as the Prime Minister describes this measure, they wish to create, instead of national sovereignties, an imperial sovereignty to which all the other nations of the earth will have to pay tribute, an imperial sovereignty which in the economic realm will help make impossible trade between the dominions of the empire and the other countries of the world. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, that raises the greatest question that has ever been raised in this parliament with regard to the future development of this country and of the British Empire of which it is a part.
The germ of all that is bound up in one of the three short sections of the bill now before us for second reading. In a word, Mr. Speaker, the issue has become one of "commonwealth
or empire." We believe in the British commonwealth as a community of nations free in their sovereign rights, free with respect to fiscal policies and all other matters, free to develop as they think best but in no way interfering with the autonomous rights of other parts. Hon. gentlemen opposite are seeking to create instead an empire, with imperial policies which ultimately will control all its parts from a common centre under an imperial sovereignty.
My right hon. friend says he will stand or fall by these agreements.
