With the closing words and sentiments expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) I fully agree. With the beginning of his speech, in which he justified his opposition to the form in which these agreements are presented, I also agree. I will not be claptrapped into voting for the agreements, even if they have tacked on to them some amendment sponsored by my good friends to my left, as the whole Liberal party did a few days ago.
As the leader of the opposition rightly stated, this is perhaps the most important piece of legislation that not only this parliament, but any parliament since confederation has been called upon to consider. I refer not so much to the trade agreements themselves as to the implications and consequences which are bound to arise from them if they are carried through. Therefore, whenever I have a chance to record my vote against these agreements, against the principles on which they are based and against their possible consequences, I will so vote, right or left, with or against any group or party in this house. I am bound to take exception, however, to the history which the leader of the opposition endeavoured to give of the so-called British preference. I am the last man to stand and speak in this house who was an eye witness to the adoption of the policy advocated by the Liberal party, not only in 1897 but from the time of the great Liberal convention held here in 1893.
But before I take that up, may I venture to make an offer to my good friend the leader of the opposition and to the leader of

If these two prize fighters will for once accept my humble umpireship, I will avail myself of my white hair to advise them to put a stop, if possible, to those personal debates and bickerings, which have multiplied themselves especially during this session, while the people of Canada are crying out, not for bantering words between two leaders but for action by the parliament of Canada.
Now I come back to the history of the Liberal party, in matters of tariff. As the leader of the opposition said this evening, the Liberals always have been in theory free traders; but in practice they acted as protectionists. It has been simply a question of degree as between the Liberals and the Conservatives. In 1893 I was present in the great rink here in Ottawa when we acclaimed one of the leaders of our party pledging his honour and that of all true Liberals in Canada, that once they came to power they would wipe out the last vestige of protection, because protection was nothing more or less than organized robbery. But when the year 1895 came, after the famous incident in the Tory party, which good old Sir Mackenzie Bowell called the "nest of traitors," the Liberals saw their chance of coming into power. Although they relied mainly on the sentiments of the people of Canada, they also required some material assistance in the way of electoral subscriptions; and therefore Mr. Prefontaine, Mr. Tarte and the late Senator Mackay went to some of the leading financiers and manufacturers of Montreal and asked for some subscriptions, whereupon they were told that the Liberal party must make a little change in its fiscal policy. So that when the Liberals had won the election, partly by prayers and partly with the money of the parties interested in the maintenance of a customs tariff, they preserved a sufficient degree of protection. They turned to the free traders of Ontario and of the west and said to them, "We have reduced the tariff on certain matters;" and then to Montreal and Toronto manufacturers they said, or whispered: "We have preserved the practice of protection, although we still stick to the faith and principle of free trade." But that was not all. They had to find a device whereby a further reduction in the tariff as against the world at large would be rendered almost impossible, and they fell upon the so-called British preference.
Now, time and again on both sides of this house, I have heard statements in regard to the British preference inaugurated in 1897-98. I was present in the house and, gullible young chap as I was, I voted for these measures.

But they were entirely different. In 1897 we offered and gave freely a reduction of the tariff, not only to the mother country for which the leader of the opposition sheds tears occasionally, but to all countries on earth that were prepared to give and were actually giving to Canada such trade advantages as would justify us in extending to them trade privileges. It was not a British preference. It was not an imperial preference. It was a reduction in duty on the part of Canada- to Great Britain for the reasons given to-night by the leader of the opposition, and to all other countries on earth who offered us equivalent advantages. The evidence is that automatically that preference applied to Germany, Holland, Belgium and various other countries that had concluded with Great Britain trade agreements under which the most favoured nation clause obliged us to give them the same treatment that we gave to the British.
Then came the jubilee of 1897. Mr. Laurier, as he was then, went to England, where he bathed in the atmosphere of imperial glory. Then he made those speeches in which he pledged the youth of Canada to fight all the battles of England, a pledge which was redeemed, without the authorization of parliament, in the month of October, 1899, by the government of Canada promising to take the money of the people of this country to help in the most infamous war that has ever been waged, according to the judgment of such men as John Morley and Edward Clarke, to name only two of them, one a Radical and one a Conservative of England. During that same year 1897, Mr. Chamberlain succeeded in making Sir Wilfrid realize, or at any rate imagine, that this preference offered to the world could be made the means of strengthening the bonds of empire. Therefore, at the next session, in 1898, true to his pledges taken in England, but contrary to his pledges given in Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government made a tripartite or three-scale tariff: one for Great Britain, because of our love for everything British; one intermediate tariff for countries that might offer us greater trade advantages than Great Britain and the British Empire; and another for the rest of the world. Two years afterwards, in the fulness of the first fits of our imperial inebriety, our sons were dying on the veldt of Africa, to enable a pack of thieves to rob two small nations of their sovereignty in order to make some money by the digging of gold and the scratching for diamonds, thereby giving rise to the judgment-made public twenty or thirty years later by Lord Newton-of the ven-

erable Lord Salisbury, who deprecated the fact that the honour of England, its treasures and its blood were spent in order to make good the speculations of the most contemptible people on earth. But, of course, Lord Salisbury had to support a policy which he hated, just as the Liberals of Canada spoke in favour of a policy which they also hated. It was then that Mr. Fielding got my dear old friend Ben Russell to stand up in the house and raise his hands to heaven, glorifying Great Britain and the empire, saying, " Let us go further in our generosity to the poor little nation to the north of Europe; let the wealthy people of Canada give of their best to England and increase the preference from 25 to 33^ per cent." On that occasion, may I say frankly to my Liberal friends, I stood up and voted with the Tories against them, because I would rather vote for a cynical Tory protectionist policy than for a hypocritical Liberal free trade policy.
Now that I have finished this little bit of history, started by the leader of the government, not quite completed but prolonged by the leader of the opposition, as regards the British preference, may I add this much to prove to my good friends on the other side of the house that my sentiments are just as broad, so far as they are concerned, as they are towards those on this side? What the leader of the opposition said to-night is absolutely true; the Conservatives voted, and I voted with them in 1900, to condemn that policy, and they condemned it at every session from 1898 to 1911. Then they came into power in 1911, raising the cry of imperial loyalty and denouncing that poor little reciprocity treaty, which was innocuous. Hands off the British Empire 1 No truck or trade with the Yankees! Oh no; we were so loyal that if we shipped a few bags of potatoes to the United States, our British hearts and our fidelity to the British Empire would go with them! Thereby they secured the defeat of the reciprocity policy and of the government, this their main concern. They came into power and remained in power ten years; and during those ten years, they maintained untouched that policy against which they had voted, against which I had voted, a policy I denounced when the Liberals were in power and when the Conservatives were in power, a policy I denounce now, for the reasons which, once more, I will sum up in five minutes.
I have said that the so-called British preference was a clever device to redeem on the one hand the pledges given by the Liberal leaders to the farmers and the consuming community, that there would be general tariff reductions. It was a still cleverer device to
reassure the interested parties, on the other hand, that the general tariff would never be touched. I have said more than once in this house, and I repeat to-night, that the safest means by which Canada will remain a protectionist country is to maintain the policy which was inaugurated by the Liberals in 1897-98, and which they pretend to maintain and to increase. I repeat that, either as a Canadian policy or as an imperial policy, so-called, the preferential policy is the cleverest -I was going to say the most devilish-device to maintain the principle and practice of protection.
The leader of the opposition has made reference to the 'conference of 1902. I was a member of the house at that time, and my dear old friend 'Sir Wilfrid Laurier kept me informed of everything that went on. I followed closely the debates of the conference. Both the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition have forgotten one vital point which has some bearing on the matter. The leader of the apposition has said rightly that the duties then existing in England had been imposed as a war measure; but he ought to know, and I think he does know, that Mr. Chamberlain intended and endeavoured to take advantage of the conference of 1902 in order to convert that policy into a permanent policy. He succeeded in getting the agree-" ment of the Liberal representatives of Canada and the acquiescence of the other dominions, or colonies, as they were then called, to his attempt to force the English to accept as a permanent policy that which had been brought into being as a war-time measure. I am speaking extemporaneously, but my memory is pretty good in spite of my days, and I think this is borne out by the closing sentence of the memorandum which was signed by Mr. Fielding and Mr. Paterson. If my right hon. friends will read that memorandum I think they will find there a threat of retaliation by Canada unless Great Britain agrees to transform that policy into a permanent bargain. Mr. Fielding was a gentleman and Mr. Paterson was a kindly old man-by the way he was a brother-in-law of the last president of the Orange Free State. Neither of them used the forcible language used by the leader of the government last August-. I do not think any of the English representatives would have found an illustration of the temper of these gentlemen upon the ranch of the Prince of Wales in Calgary. Nevertheless, the threat was there and the warning was given that if the bargain was not fulfilled by the British government, the Canadian government would revise its policy. It is there in black and white for those who know

Do the leaders of the opposition and the government, do my Liberal and Progressive friends believe that if Mr. Chamberlain had carried out 'his so-called tariff reform policy in 1905 and granted preferences all around to the British dominions, the British dominions would not have responded according to the promises made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier? Had that happened, we would have been tied up thirty years ago to a policy which has been denounced right along by myself both in words and in votes, and by what little influence 1 can exercise in my little corner of this country.
The house is now being asked to pronounce itself in favour of the principle of preferential treatment, either as between Great Britain and Canada, or as between the various component parts of the empire. We are being asked to play into the hands of the interests of this country who want to preserve the general tariff high enough to protect themselves against foreign competition. We are also being asked to play into the hands of those who, as the leader of the opposition well said, desire to transform the British Empire into a replica- of the old Roman empire or of the German Reidh, These imperialists, by appealing to sordid interests, are endeavouring, under the pretence of trade, to put through principles of political and military unity which they could not get first hand.
This policy brought about Mr. Chamberlain's temporary defeat; but it has produced, this year, a victory of which the leader of the government is entitled to be proud from his own point of view. I am the last man to belittle his object, to belittle his person, to belittle his aims, to belittle his endeavours and his success; but let me tell him that as a Canadian, as a true lover of British institutions-I will not say that I am prepared to shed my blood for Great Britain; I will not take that pose because no one would believe me-I want our relations to last as long as possible; and that is precisely what this policy threatens.
I turn now to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition and advise him to stand solidly upon the ground he took during the last fifteen minutes of his speech and Stop offering himself to the people of the empire as the future wet-nurse of poor old England.

Hear, hear.
{Mr. Bourassa.]

But I say also to my Conservative friends: Stop posing before the people of Canada as being obliged to milk-feed for all time the suckling pigs of industry of this country. I say to the leader of the government, who is big enough, who is intelligent enough, to reach a position in the history of Canada never surpassed in the past: For heaven's sake, cease thinking about doing all you think you can do! Let him cease concerning himself about the policies of one-quarter of the population of the earth; let him not try to outdo Ghandi and Hertzog and Cosgrave and De Valera and all the other statesmen of the empire. He will govern Canada more effectively by remaining true to himself. I ask him not to be so much concerned about the disaster which will befall this country if the manufacturers who have fattened themselves at our expense for so many years, are forced to give back to the community a little of their ill-earned profits.
Mr. Speaker, I beg your pardon for the heated manner in which I have spoken. I have not spoken through any rancour, but with the sincere object of shedding the light of truth upon the somewhat distorted historical recitals we have heard during the last month.
